clue.text: Error in play that’s an allegory for an alligator?

blocks.note: first meaning: a verbal slip named after a character in a stage comedy, so an error born in a play
second meaning, by example: Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's The Rivals spoke of 'an allegory on the banks of the Nile'

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a fable can stand in for a reptile, a muddle during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's comedy The Rivals, whose famous slip was 'as headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile', meaning alligator.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names any ludicrous misuse of a similar-sounding word, named after that stage character who habitually made such slips.

clue.text: Very drunk son on island beginning to notice a grave mistake

indicators.note: a beginning is the start of something, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: British slang: 'mortal' or 'mortal drunk' means hopelessly drunk
S is the standard abbreviation for son
I is the abbreviation for island
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A drunken son stranded on an island starts to realise he has made a terrible error.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang someone 'mortal' is blind drunk. 'On' simply strings the pieces together in order: MORTAL + S + I + N.
explanation.definitionFit: In Catholic teaching a deadly sin destroys grace in the soul, the gravest kind of wrongdoing, so the phrase works as a serious error.

clue.text: March is delayed by this complicated pay deal

indicators.note: something complicated is tangled up, so these letters come out in a muddled order

blocks.note: the seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A protest march is postponed because negotiations over a wage settlement have become tangled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' looks like a demonstration being held up by talks, but it is the month, which starts a day later in a leap year.
explanation.definitionFit: The extra calendar date of 29 February sits before the third month, pushing its arrival back by one day every four years.

clue.text: Sausage spatter every second from corn oil

indicators.note: taking every second item means skipping one and keeping the next, all the way along

blocks.note: to pepper is to spatter or sprinkle all over
the even-placed letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A sausage frying in corn oil spits and spatters.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the second, fourth and sixth letters of 'corn oil' gives O, N, I.
explanation.definitionFit: This spicy Italian-American cured salami is a type of dried sausage, familiar as a pizza topping.

clue.text: One eyeing river and lake that I must get around, going north

indicators.note: to get around something is to surround it, so one piece goes outside another
in a down clue, going north means travelling upwards, so the letters are read bottom to top

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for river
the ego is the self, the 'I'
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Someone watching a river and a lake must walk around them heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: The self is the ego, the 'I' of psychology. In a down entry 'going north' means the built word is read from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who looks at another person, often lecherously or intently, is one who stares, eyeing them.

clue.text: One of us reported hotel drink

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we go by what is heard

blocks.note: a hotel is an inn and cider is an apple drink; together they are heard as one word

explanation.surface: A guest phones in to say what they had to drink at the hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: INN plus CIDER, said aloud, runs together into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of an inner circle or group, someone on the inside, is 'one of us' as opposed to an outsider.

clue.text: Satellite leaking nitrogen concerning BBC astronomer

indicators.note: whatever leaks escapes from its container, so a letter is lost

blocks.note: the Moon is Earth's satellite
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen
re means 'concerning' or 'about'

explanation.surface: A space satellite springs a nitrogen leak, worrying a TV stargazer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concerning' looks like worry in the surface, but it is the short word for 'about' used in letters and memos.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Patrick Moore presented the BBC television programme The Sky at Night for over fifty years, Britain's best-known stargazer.

clue.text: Medic leaving xylophone for Callas?

definitions.note: a surname standing for the soprano's first name

indicators.note: whoever is leaving goes away, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification
a marimba is a large wooden xylophone

explanation.surface: A doctor quits playing xylophone in favour of an opera diva.
explanation.walkthrough: MARIMBA minus the M and B leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Greek-American soprano was named Maria Callas, so her surname points to her first name.

clue.text: Novel‘s drama slowly unfolding

indicators.note: unfolding opens something out into a new shape, so the letters are spread into another order

blocks.note: the eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A book's story unfolds as a slow-moving drama.
explanation.walkthrough: The ‘s stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Virginia Woolf's 1925 book, following a society hostess through a single June day in London, is a famous work of fiction.

clue.text: Backsliding hack is gone after hour’s shift

indicators.note: backsliding means slipping backwards, so the letters run the other way
after means following, so the piece before this word is placed second

blocks.note: to lop is to hack or chop off
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hour
food that has gone bad is off

explanation.surface: A lapsed journalist has vanished after an hour on duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places OFF behind H. 'Hack' looks like a journalist, and 'shift' like a work period, but it is the definition in its sense of getting through or disposing of.
explanation.definitionFit: To get through food or stock quickly, consuming or disposing of it entirely, is to shift it in informal British usage.

clue.text: Gold medallist could be me or Adam

blocks.note: first meaning: whoever comes first wins gold
second meaning: 'me' belongs to the grammatical form for the speaker, and Adam was the first human being

explanation.surface: Someone muses that they, or a friend called Adam, could win an Olympic gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Me or Adam' covers two senses at once: 'me' is a first-person pronoun in grammar, and Adam was literally the first man.
explanation.definitionFit: A gold winner is the one who finishes ahead of everyone, and the grammar term covers I and me, the speaker's own pronouns.

clue.text: Wrap up finale for Chris Rock

indicators.note: a finale is the closing part, so only the end letter is used

blocks.note: the closing letter of the name
to waddle is to walk with a rocking, side-to-side gait

explanation.surface: The comedian Chris Rock ends his show with a wrap-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chris Rock' reads as the comedian, but the name only lends its last letter and 'Rock' is a verb for swaying gait.
explanation.definitionFit: Swaddling a baby means wrapping it tightly in cloth, so the verb means to wrap up snugly.

clue.text: Does perhaps drink with twisted straw

indicators.note: something twisted is turned round, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: red is a glass of red wine
a reed is a hollow stalk, a natural straw

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person is drinking through a bendy straw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like the verb, but it is the plural of doe, a female deer; 'perhaps' signals an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Female deer are called does, and Britain's largest native species is one example of an animal whose females bear that name.

clue.text: Examine article, the leader in Sunday Express

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: 'a' is the indefinite article
the opening letter of the day
to express something is to say it

explanation.surface: Scrutinise a newspaper feature and the editorial in a Sunday tabloid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader' and 'Sunday Express' suggest a newspaper editorial; the Sunday Express is a real British paper, but here 'Express' is just a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To assay metal or ore is to test it for purity, a technical word for analysing or examining something.

clue.text: Eagle-eyed Robin runs away, not at home with Batman, say

indicators.note: whatever goes away is no longer present, so a letter drops out
'not' cancels what follows, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
someone at home is in
a batman is an army officer's personal servant; 'say' marks an example

explanation.surface: Sharp-sighted Robin flees, leaving the house with his crime-fighting partner Batman.
explanation.walkthrough: Robin and Batman make a superhero pair, but a batman is also a British officer's orderly. ROBIN loses R and IN, leaving OB.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with keen vision like a bird of prey notices everything, which is what being quick to notice details means.

clue.text: Second mate’s relaxed in vessel

indicators.note: something relaxed has loosened from its fixed form, so the letters fall into another order

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
the letters to rearrange
what is in fashion is hip

explanation.surface: The second mate takes it easy aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second mate' is a ship's officer, but 'Second' only gives S, and 'in' is not a container signal but a word meaning fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: A large ship driven by steam engines is a seagoing craft, and a vessel is the general word for any ship.

clue.text: Jazz producer?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who records and produces jazz music
setter's reading: Jazz is a modern variety of eating fruit, so its producer is whatever it grows on

explanation.walkthrough: Jazz is a crisp red-skinned eating variety bred in New Zealand; the question mark warns that 'producer' is meant literally, as what bears the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchard fruit like the Jazz variety grows on this plant, which literally produces the crop each season.

clue.text: Line cut in hem, fancy one?

definitions.note: a number standing for a time of day

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are worked into a new arrangement

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for line
the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A dressmaker asks whether to cut a line into an ornate hem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' wants to be an instruction to remove letters, but it is part of the fodder. 'One' means one o'clock, a typical midday meal hour.
explanation.definitionFit: One o'clock in the afternoon is a typical hour for the midday meal, so the number is an example of that period.

clue.text: Persist in talking about Lazarenko’s last dart

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another
the last of something is its end, so only the final letter is taken

blocks.note: to harp on is to keep talking about something tediously
the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: Someone keeps going on about the final dart thrown by a player named Lazarenko.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like part of the phrase for nagging, but it is the signal to put the single letter inside that phrase, between its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbed spear thrown or fired at whales is a missile, and a dart is any pointed projectile hurled at a target.

clue.text: Heading off for Beatles single and extremely expensive album

indicators.note: a heading is the top item, and taking it off removes the opening letter
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: Help! was a 1965 Beatles single
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A collector trades a Beatles single for a very costly LP.
explanation.walkthrough: HELP loses its H. The answer is LP written out as a word, as in 'an LP'.
explanation.definitionFit: An LP is a long-playing vinyl record, and spelling the letters out phonetically gives a crossword-friendly word for such a record.

clue.text: Graduates wearing frameless lenses in a group

indicators.note: what you wear goes around you, so one piece is wrapped by another
a frame is the border, so without it only the inside letters remain

blocks.note: MAs are Masters of Arts, holders of a degree
the word with its first and last letters gone

explanation.surface: Graduates in rimless glasses stand around together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frameless lenses' paints rimless spectacles, but it means the word with its outer letters trimmed away. MA is a Master of Arts degree.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase, borrowed into English, means all together as one body, everybody at once.

clue.text: Roller the German reversed and moved to and fro

indicators.note: reversed means turned backwards, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: a roller is a big rolling wave
der is German for 'the'

explanation.surface: A German driver backs up his Rolls-Royce, shunting it back and forth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roller' suggests a Rolls-Royce car, but it is a large sea wave.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that flickers or sways unsteadily, swinging from side to side, has shifted back and forth in place.

clue.text: Soft membrane defensive lumpfish protects

indicators.note: to protect is to shield or enclose, so the letters sit enclosed in the words around them

blocks.note: runs across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A lumpfish on the defensive guards its soft skin.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle the end of 'defensive' and the start of 'lumpfish'.
explanation.definitionFit: In anatomy and biology a veil-like tissue, such as the soft palate at the back of the mouth, is given this Latin name.

clue.text: Approach chauffeur

blocks.note: first meaning: the private road leading up to a house
second meaning: to take someone somewhere by car

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like verbs, but the first is a noun: the approach road to a house.
explanation.definitionFit: A private road up to a house is called its approach, and a chauffeur's job is to transport passengers by car.

clue.text: Supporters of helpless maid, Cinders

blocks.note: read 'help-less': a maid with her aid (help) taken away leaves one letter
embers are the glowing cinders of a fire

explanation.surface: Fans rally behind poor Cinderella, the helpless kitchen maid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Helpless' must be split as 'help less', removing a word for help from the maid. Cinders is Cinderella's nickname, but here it means ashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying subscribers who belong to a club or party back it, so they count as its backers or fans.

clue.text: Cry over dream, somewhat cowardly

blocks.note: to yell is to cry out
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over
a dream is a wish or hope

explanation.surface: Someone a little timid weeps over a lost dream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like a link meaning 'about', but it gives O, the scorecard abbreviation for an over in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow is slang for lacking courage, and the -ish ending softens it to 'rather', so the word means a bit lily-livered.

clue.text: Good to avoid singer at sea – this one?

definitions.text: Good to avoid singer at sea – this one?

indicators.note: to avoid something is to keep clear of it, so that letter is left out
at sea means confused and adrift, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sailors are warned that it is wise to keep away from one particular singer out on the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: SINGER drops G and the rest is scrambled. Read whole, the clue also describes the creature: a sea singer that sailors would do well to avoid.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth these sea nymphs lured sailors onto rocks with song, the very marine vocalist mariners should steer clear of.

clue.text: Shelf Wolf Hall?

blocks.note: first meaning: the ledge above a fireplace
second meaning, read as two words: a work written by Hilary Mantel

explanation.walkthrough: Wolf Hall is Hilary Mantel's Booker-winning novel about Thomas Cromwell, so it is a 'Mantel piece'; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The ledge above a hearth is a fireplace shelf, and a novel by that author is one of her written works.
